h1: The 8 Best NAS for Mac and Time Machine Backup of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best NAS for Time Machine 2026: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: eight NAS drives for Mac Time Machine backup, from budget 2-bay units to a 4-bay RAID box, with advice on speed and Mac count.
summary: The Synology DS223 is our top pick because its Time Machine setup is the least fiddly. The QNAP TS-264 is best for several Macs backing up at once, and the UGREEN DH2300 is the budget route for a single Mac. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is the pick for RAID and three or more Macs.
intro: The usual NAS mistake for Mac owners is buying on drive bays and ignoring the first backup. Time Machine writes a huge initial copy, and a slow network port or a weak processor turns that into a multi-day job.

We ranked eight diskless NAS units, all of which list SMB3 Time Machine support, using the spec sheets and what owners report. Setup friction, network speed, processor headroom, multi-Mac handling and price bucket set the order, since a backup box is only useful if it keeps running without attention. Remember that none of these ship with drives.

products.name: Synology DS223 Home & Office Backup Hub
products.verdict: The easiest Time Machine setup of the group.
products.description:
The DS223 is a 2-bay diskless NAS with a built-in Time Machine shared-folder wizard using SMB3 and Bonjour. You can set a quota for each Mac in the same flow, and RAID 1 is supported. It is priced from $200 to $500.

It ranks first because a household's biggest headache is setup, and this unit smooths it. It sits above the QNAP TS-264 since it asks less of you, but the tradeoff is fixed RAM that you cannot upgrade, so it has less headroom for extra services.

Choose it for a home with two or three Macs that just wants backups to work. The caveat is that the hardware is basic, so it is a backup hub rather than a media powerhouse.
products.idealFor: Homes with two or three Macs that want simple backups.
products.skipIf: You want a NAS that also runs heavy extra apps.

products.name: QNAP TS-264-8G-US 2-Bay Desktop NAS
products.verdict: The most memory in a 2-bay, for several Macs at once.
products.description:
A 2-bay desktop NAS with 8GB of RAM, the most for a 2-bay on this list, plus 2.5GbE networking and SMB3 Time Machine shares that support multiple Macs. It runs QNAP QTS with its full app store and sits in the $200 to $500 bucket.

It ranks below the Synology only because setup takes more steps, but it ranks above the other QNAP because the memory and app support give real room for overlapping backups. That headroom is the main tradeoff you are buying.

It suits households where two or more Macs back up at the same time. The caveat is a busier operating system, which is more to learn than the Synology.
products.idealFor: Households with two or more Macs backing up together.
products.skipIf: You want the simplest possible setup.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP2800
products.verdict: More processor power for big MacBook Pro archives.
products.description:
The DXP2800 is a 2-bay NAS with higher-performance hardware aimed at content creators. It supports SMB3 Time Machine shares and snapshot-based versioning, and the CPU is chosen to handle large sparse bundles. It is priced from $200 to $500.

It ranks below the QNAP TS-264 because that unit lists more memory and a clearer multi-Mac story, and above the cheaper UGREEN since the processor handles bigger archives. The tradeoff is cost against the DH2300.

Buy it if your MacBook Pro has a large internal drive and the backup archive will be sizable. The caveat is that you rely on UGREEN's app ecosystem, which is newer than Synology's.
products.idealFor: MacBook Pro owners with large drives and big archives.
products.skipIf: You only back up a small, single-Mac drive.

products.name: TERRAMASTER F2-425
products.verdict: An Intel quad-core NAS that does more than backups.
products.description:
A 2-bay NAS with an Intel x86 quad-core CPU, 4GB of RAM and 2.5GbE LAN, with SMB3 Time Machine share support and a diskless enclosure. It is priced from $200 to $500.

It ranks fourth because it offers solid hardware but has less mature Mac-focused setup than the Synology. Compared with the QNAP TS-264 it has half the memory, which is the clearest tradeoff.

It suits buyers who want Time Machine plus a few other light services. The caveat is that Mac backups are one feature here, not the guided focus.
products.idealFor: Buyers who want Time Machine plus other light tasks.
products.skipIf: You want a wizard-driven, set-and-forget backup.

products.name: QNAP TS-216G-US 2-Bay 2.5GbE Desktop NAS
products.verdict: A 2.5GbE port aimed at shortening the first big backup.
products.description:
A 2-bay desktop NAS with a 2.5GbE port, SMB3 Time Machine share support, the QTS operating system and standard 2-bay RAID. It is priced from $200 to $500.

It ranks below the TS-264 because the listing gives no memory figure and fewer multi-Mac details. What it keeps is the fast network port, which matters most during the first full backup.

Choose it if your home network already runs 2.5GbE and speed on day one is the goal. The caveat is that on a gigabit network the faster port brings no benefit.
products.idealFor: Owners with a 2.5GbE network wanting a fast first backup.

products.name: Asustor Drivestor 2 Gen 2 AS1202T
products.verdict: 2.5GbE speed in the lower price bucket.
products.description:
A 2-bay NAS with a quad-core 1.7GHz CPU, 1GB of DDR4 RAM and 2.5GbE networking, running ADM with SMB3 Time Machine shares and 4K media server support. This one runs $100 to $200.

It ranks below the Intel-based TERRAMASTER because it has a quarter of the memory, and above the UGREEN DH2300 since it brings 2.5GbE at a similar bucket. The tradeoff is thin memory for the price.

It suits first-time NAS buyers who want a fast port without a bigger spend. The caveat is the 1GB of RAM, which limits how much else the unit can do.
products.idealFor: First-time NAS buyers who want 2.5GbE for less.
products.skipIf: You plan to run many apps on the box.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DH2300
products.verdict: A low-cost enclosure for one Mac's backups.
products.description:
A 2-bay diskless NAS supporting up to 64TB of total capacity, with SMB3 Time Machine share support and an entry-level CPU and RAM tier. This one runs $100 to $200.

It ranks near the bottom because the hardware is entry level, so it has little room for multiple Macs or other tasks. Its place above the DXP4800 Plus is purely price: it undercuts the rest of the list.

Buy it for a single Mac on a tight budget. The caveat is limited headroom, and the capacity ceiling matters only if you fill both bays with large drives.
products.idealFor: Single-Mac households on a tight budget.
products.skipIf: Several Macs back up to it at once.

products.award: Best for RAID and Many Macs
products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP4800 Plus
products.verdict: Four bays and real RAID, if you can justify the spend.
products.description:
This four-bay enclosure ships without drives and runs an Intel Pentium Gold 8505 with five cores. It offers RAID 5, 6 and 10 and copes with several Time Machine shares running together. It has the highest capacity ceiling on the list and sits in the $500 and up bucket.

It ranks last only because few households need it; the price bucket is the highest and the extra bays go unused for a one or two Mac home. Against the Synology, it trades simplicity for scale.

Choose it for three or more Macs and a wish for RAID flexibility. The caveat is cost, and the need to buy four drives to use it fully.
products.idealFor: Households with three or more Macs wanting RAID.
products.skipIf: You have one or two Macs and a modest budget.

whatMatters.detail: Time Machine is Apple's built-in backup, and a NAS must expose an SMB3 share for it. Without proper support, backups can fail or be unreliable. Look for SMB3 and Time Machine named in the specs.
A 2.5GbE port moves data faster than gigabit, which helps the first large backup. It only helps if your router and Mac support it. Check your own network before paying for it.
RAID spreads or mirrors data across drives so one failure does not erase your backup. A 2-bay offers RAID 1, and a 4-bay unlocks RAID 5, 6 and 10. Check the listed RAID levels.
The processor and memory handle the sparse bundles Time Machine creates and any extra services. Weak hardware slows several simultaneous backups. Look for the RAM figure in the listing.
Every unit here ships without drives, so you pay separately. Budget for drives sized to roughly two times your Mac's used storage. Read the listing for the word diskless.

faq.q: Do these NAS drives come with disks?
faq.a: No. All eight are listed as diskless or without drives mentioned, so plan to buy drives separately.

faq.q: What is the most common Time Machine mistake?
faq.a: Buying drives too small. A backup needs room for history, so size the capacity well above your Mac's used storage.
Only if your router and Mac support it. Otherwise the port runs at gigabit and you gain nothing.

faq.q: How do I set up Time Machine on a NAS?
faq.a: Create an SMB3 Time Machine share on the NAS, then pick it in macOS Time Machine settings. The Synology DS223 includes a wizard for this.

faq.q: Should I use RAID for backups?
faq.a: RAID 1 protects against one drive failing, which is sensible for a backup. It does not replace keeping another copy elsewhere.

faq.q: Can several Macs share one NAS?
faq.a: Yes, with separate shares or quotas. The QNAP TS-264 and UGREEN DXP4800 Plus are listed for multiple Macs.

finalTake: The Synology DS223 is the safest buy for most Mac households because it removes setup friction. The QNAP TS-264 is better when several Macs back up at once, and the UGREEN DH2300 handles a single Mac cheaply. Choose the DXP4800 Plus only when you truly need four bays and RAID.
